code.title: Class vs object: one blueprint, separate instances

followUps:
Per class. Method bytecode is stored once, in the class's metadata, and every object shares it. An object holds only its field values plus a header pointing to its class.

Example: 1,000 Dog objects with 2 fields each hold 2,000 field values, but bark() exists once. When you call d.bark(), the JVM passes d as the hidden this argument, so the same code works on different data.

Three: two new objects and one string literal. The literal is created once and kept in the string pool.

For example new Person(new Name(), "Ana") allocates a Person, a Name, and the literal "Ana" is a pooled String that exists once for the whole JVM, however many times that text appears. Note new String("Ana") would add one more heap object, so count the keyword uses plus any distinct literal.

code.title: Order of events in new Dog("Rex")

followUps:
Yes, sometimes. If escape analysis proves the object never leaves the method, the JIT compiler can skip the heap allocation entirely.

It does this by scalar replacement: the object's fields become plain local variables in registers or on the stack, and no object header exists. Example: in a loop calling new Point(i, i).sum() a million times, a hot, inlined loop may allocate nothing at all. It works only after JIT compilation and only if the object does not escape (is not stored in a field, returned, or passed to non-inlined code).

The object is never handed back, so d is never assigned. The half-built object becomes garbage that nobody can reach.

The exception travels up the call stack. The memory was already allocated, but the garbage collector frees it later. If super() or field initializers ran first, their side effects (opened resources, registered listeners) stay, so constructors that acquire resources should clean up themselves in a try/catch before rethrowing. A failure in a static initializer is different: it gives ExceptionInInitializerError.

code.title: Proof that Java is pass-by-value

followUps:
A String parameter is passed by value like everything else; it only looks different because String is immutable. You cannot change the object through the copied reference.

Example: void f(String s) { s = s + "!"; } builds a new String and points the local s at it; the caller still holds "hi". With a StringBuilder parameter, sb.append("!") mutates the shared object, so the caller sees the change. The rules are identical; only mutability differs.

Return one object that holds both values, because Java methods return a single value.

Options: a small record Pair(int a, int b) (best, type-safe), a two-element array (quick, untyped), or an existing type such as Map.Entry. Example:

record MinMax(int min, int max) {}
static MinMax range(int[] a) {
    int lo = a[0], hi = a[0];
    for (int v : a) { lo = Math.min(lo, v); hi = Math.max(hi, v); }
    return new MinMax(lo, hi);
}

code.title: Default constructor and when it disappears

followUps:
Not exactly. A no-arg constructor is any constructor with no parameters; the default constructor is the one the compiler writes for you when you declare none.

Behaviour is the same (it just calls super()), but if you write Foo() {} yourself it is an ordinary constructor, not the default one. A difference you can see: you can give your own a body, change its access, or add validation. The generated one also appears in the class file only when no constructor was declared.

It gets the same access as the class: a public class gets a public default constructor, a package-private class gets a package-private one.

Examples: public class A {} has public A(); class B {} has package-private B(); a protected nested class gets a protected one. An enum's default constructor is private. This means a package-private class with only the default constructor cannot be built from another package, even if you think it is open.

code.title: Constructor chaining with this() and super()

followUps:
Because the object does not exist yet: the instance methods and fields cannot be used safely before the parent part has been built.

The compiler rejects this(compute()) if compute() is an instance method, because it would run on a half-built this before super() finished. Use a static helper or a parameter instead:

Foo() { this(defaultSize()); }   // static int defaultSize()
Foo(int n) { this.n = n; }

Static methods and constants are fine because they need no instance.

Once. Instance initializers and field initializers run only in the constructor that calls super(...), not in one that delegates with this(...).

Example: A() { this(5); } and A(int n) { ... }. new A() runs A(), which jumps to A(int); the field initializers and blocks run at the start of A(int) (after its implicit super()) exactly one time, then the bodies finish innermost first. The compiler guarantees this to avoid double initialisation.

code.title: Five uses of this

followUps:
It means the object being built is visible to other code before its constructor has finished, so others may see fields still at their defaults.

Example: a constructor does bus.register(this) as its first line. If an event fires on another thread, the listener runs while this.name is still null. Dangerous causes: registering listeners, starting threads, storing this in a static, and calling overridable methods. Fix it by finishing construction and then publishing from a static factory method.

In an instance method or constructor, this is the hidden first argument, stored in local variable slot 0.

The compiler turns obj.f(x) into a call where obj is slot 0 and x is slot 1. Bytecode aload_0 loads this. In a static method slot 0 holds the first real parameter instead, which is why a static method cannot use this. Slot 0 is not reassigned by Java code, so this = other does not compile.

code.title: Static field, block and method

followUps:
Yes, it compiles, but it is misleading: the compiler only uses the declared type of the reference and treats it as a static access.

Example: Ticket t = null; int n = t.issued; works and reads the class's single field, with no NullPointerException. IDEs warn about it. A static method cannot, however, touch an instance field directly (name) because there is no this; it needs an object passed in: static String show(Person p) { return p.name; }.

In the heap, as part of the class's java.lang.Class object. Before Java 8 they were in PermGen.

Java 8 removed PermGen and moved class metadata to Metaspace (native memory), but the static field values themselves live in the Class mirror object on the heap. So a static reference such as static List cache keeps its objects alive for as long as the class stays loaded, which is a common source of memory leaks.

code.title: Static methods: overload, hide, not override

followUps:
Overloading is allowed and main is just an ordinary method name. The JVM looks for the exact signature public static void main(String[]) and ignores others.

Example: you can also write static void main(int x) or main(String a, String b); they are plain overloads you must call yourself. Only the String[] version is the entry point. (Java 21 preview also allows instance main methods, but the classic signature is always accepted.)

Nothing bad: it runs normally, because a static call is resolved from the declared type at compile time and does not use the object.

Example: Child c = null; c.who(); calls Child.who() with no exception. An instance method call on null would throw NullPointerException. This is another reason to call statics through the class name, so the code reads honestly.

code.title: Initialization order in a class hierarchy

followUps:
When you only use a compile-time constant, or touch an inherited static field through a subclass, or merely declare a variable or array of the class.

Example: reading Consts.X where static final int X = 10 never runs Consts's static block, because 10 is inlined. Reading Child.shared, declared in Parent, runs Parent's block only. A static block also does not run if the class is never actively used at all.

Take a class with a static block that prints, and a main inside it: the static block prints first, then main runs.

The JVM must initialise the main class before calling main. Example: static { System.out.println("A"); } public static void main(String[] a) { System.out.println("B"); } prints A then B. (If a static block throws, the program fails before main even starts.) With a hierarchy, the parent's static blocks print before the child's.

code.title: Access levels shown via reflection

followUps:
Yes, but only on objects of your own subclass type, not on a plain parent-type object.

Say Parent in package a has a protected void f(), and Child in package b extends it. Inside Child, this.f() and otherChild.f() compile, but new Parent().f() or Parent p = ...; p.f() does not. The reason is that the access is granted through inheritance, so the reference must be of the subclass type or lower.

With modules, public only means visible to code in modules that the module explicitly exports the package to; the module boundary comes first.

If package com.acme.internal is not exported in module-info.java, its public classes cannot be used from other modules, even by reflection unless the package is also opens. So inside a module public behaves as before, but across modules a public class is hidden unless you write exports com.acme.api;.

code.title: Weak getters/setters vs real encapsulation

followUps:
Immutable objects cannot be changed after construction, so there is no invalid state to guard and no setter to misuse.

Example: a record Money(long cents, String currency) validated once in its constructor stays valid forever and is safe to share between threads or return from getters without copying. Mutable classes need every method to protect the invariants; immutable ones need only the constructor. The cost is creating a new object for each change.

A defensive copy is your own private copy of a mutable object, made so outsiders cannot change your internals. It is needed on input too, because the caller still holds a reference.

Example: Period(Date start) that stores this.start = start lets the caller later call start.setTime(0) and corrupt you. Use this.start = new Date(start.getTime()), and return copies (or List.copyOf / unmodifiable views) from getters. Copy first, then validate the copy, to avoid a race between check and use.

No. An import is only a compile-time shortcut for writing short names; it loads nothing and has no runtime cost.

Writing import java.util.*; does not load every class in the package. Classes are loaded lazily when the JVM first needs them. The compiled bytecode refers to full names, so import java.util.List; and writing java.util.List in the code produce the same class file.

Because the Java language has no syntax to name a class in the unnamed (default) package from a named package; the import must contain a package name.

So a class Util with no package line cannot be imported by com.acme.App. The fix is to put Util into a package. This is one reason real code should never use the default package, which is meant only for small examples and quick tests.

code.title: Three thread-safe singletons

followUps:
Because without it another thread can see a non-null reference to a half-constructed object, due to instruction reordering.

inst = new Dcl() is really three steps: allocate, run the constructor, assign the reference. The JIT or CPU may assign before the constructor finishes. A second thread passing the unlocked if (inst == null) check then uses an object whose fields are still defaults. volatile forbids that reordering and gives a happens-before edge.

Deserialization builds a brand new object through a path that skips your private constructor, so the "single" instance is no longer single.

If a singleton class implements Serializable, reading it back from a stream creates a second object. Fix it with a readResolve() method that returns the real instance: private Object readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }. An enum singleton avoids the problem because the JVM guarantees one instance per enum constant during deserialization.

code.title: This escape during construction

followUps:
Because the new thread can start running before the constructor finishes, and see a partly built object.

Example: Worker() { new Thread(this).start(); this.config = load(); }. The thread may read config as null. A subclass is even worse, as its fields are not set yet when the parent constructor runs. Create the object first, then call a start() method (or use a static factory), so construction is complete before another thread is involved.

Safe publication means making a finished object visible to other threads with a guarantee that they see all its fields. A volatile write, a final field, a lock, or a thread-safe collection all give it.

Example: after volatile Config cfg; cfg = new Config(...); any thread reading cfg sees the fully set fields, because the volatile write happens-before the read. A final field gives the same promise for its own value, as long as this did not escape.

code.title: When a class is initialised (and when not)

followUps:
Because the compiler copies the constant value into every caller's bytecode when it compiles, so the callers never read the library at runtime.

Example: the library says static final int MAX = 10. A caller compiled earlier has the literal 10 in its class file. If you ship a new JAR with MAX = 20 but do not recompile the caller, it still uses 10. The fix is to recompile callers, or make the value non-constant (for example static final int MAX = Integer.parseInt("20")).

Each class holds an initialisation lock while its static block runs. If two classes need each other in their static blocks and two threads start them in opposite order, each waits for the other forever.

Example: thread 1 starts initialising A, whose static block uses B; thread 2 starts initialising B, whose static block uses A. Thread 1 holds A and waits for B, thread 2 holds B and waits for A. Avoid cross-references between static initializers, and keep them tiny.
